supreme-court-legal.quote:
#BREAKING: Over public dissents from Justices Thomas and Alito, #SCOTUS *denies* the Trump administration’s request for a stay in the mail-in ballots case.

The USPS Rule will remain blocked—almost certainly through the midterms.

1) it’s not Kavanaugh; it’s the full Court.

2) the thing that needed to be stayed was the district court TRO, not anything the Eighth Circuit did; that’s now stayed until and unless #SCOTUS does something different; so

3) no matter what the Eighth Circuit does next, it won’t change the status quo.
It’s not formally moot, just practically moot. It therefore seems silly to me to expedite the appeal, but it won’t have any practical significance until and unless #SCOTUS changes its mind.
This was a *grant* of emergency relief, something individual justices virtually *never* do on their own anymore. The first one was a *denial,* which is often handled “in chambers.”

I'd encourage you to read the piece. I'm not arguing for a "free pass"; I'm arguing that we're only making things worse if we (wrongly) convince ourselves that law and legal constraints simply don't matter anymore.

What did we learn from the Supreme Court's three-sentence Monday night ruling leaving on hold the Trump administration's effort to interfere with mail-in voting?

Quite a lot, as it turns out—and at least some of it is good:

Among other things, this means that, even if #SCOTUS *grants* a stay of Judge Talwani’s earlier injunction against the USPS rule (which seems increasingly unlikely), the rule would *still* not go into effect; the Court would have to freeze *this* injunction, too.
